articles.summary: Candidato do PSD ao governo de Santa Catarina cumpriu agenda de campanha nesta segunda-feira (7) em Florianópolis.
articles.body:
O candidato ao governo de Santa Catarina João Rodrigues (PSD) cumpriu agenda de campanha nesta segunda-feira (7) em Florianópolis. — Foto: NSC TV/Reprodução

O candidato ao governo de Santa Catarina João Rodrigues ( PSD ) cumpriu agenda de campanha nesta segunda-feira (7) em Florianópolis .

Ele começou o dia em um encontro com apoiadores no bairro Agronômica. No local, o candidato conversou com alguns moradores sobre as reivindicações da comunidade.

Questionado pela NSC TV sobre as ações que pretende adotar para melhorar a balneabilidade em Santa Catarina, respondeu:

"Nós temos o maior problema que atinge a balneabilidade de todas as praias de Santa Catarina que é o saneamento básico. E quem é que está faltando com isso é a empresa responsável, que é a Casan. Então, a medida necessária é a privatização da Casan imediatamente e exigir da nova empresa os serviços o mais rápido possível."

Ao longo do dia, João Rodrigues também gravou programas eleitorais.

🔍 A campanha eleitoral de 2026 iniciou no dia 16 de agosto em todo o país. Desde esta data, candidatos estão autorizados a pedir votos e realizar comícios, caminhadas, debates e divulgar suas propostas em rádio, TV e internet, seguindo as regras estabelecidas pela Justiça Eleitoral.

articles.title: Alerta de temporal em Goiás atinge 160 cidades nesta terça-feira | G1
articles.standfirst: Cimehgo prevê possibilidade de chuvas intensas, rajadas de vento, raios e granizo. Frente fria reduz temperaturas em algumas regiões, mas não deve provocar frio intenso.
articles.summary: Alerta de temporal em Goiás prevê chuvas intensas e granizo em 160 cidades, enquanto a frente fria reduz as temperaturas em Goiânia e no interior.
articles.body:
Goiás tem alerta para a formação de tempestades nesta terça-feira (8), segundo o Centro de Informações Meteorológicas e Hidrológicas de Goiás (Cimehgo). O órgão aponta risco potencial em 160 dos 246 municípios do estado, incluindo Goiânia , Aparecida de Goiânia , Anápolis , Rio Verde , Jataí , Catalão , Trindade e cidades do Entorno do Distrito Federal.

Segundo o gerente do Cimehgo, André Amorim, as chuvas continuam muito irregulares pelo estado e podem atingir pontos isolados com maior intensidade. Mesmo com o deslocamento da frente fria em direção ao oceano, outros sistemas ainda favorecem o aumento da nebulosidade em Goiás. Combinada ao calor, essa condição mantém a possibilidade de tempestades isoladas em diferentes regiões.

O boletim do Cimehgo prevê para terça-feira sol com variação de nebulosidade em todas as regiões. O avanço da frente fria pelo Sudeste do país favorece o aumento das nuvens e a ocorrência de chuvas que podem vir acompanhadas de rajadas de vento, raios e, eventualmente, granizo. O órgão também alerta para ventos que podem ultrapassar os 60 km/h.

Chuva atinge diferentes regiões de Goiás nesta segunda (7); Cimehgo mantém alerta para formação de tempestades — Foto: Diomício Gomes/O Popular

O prognóstico do Cimehgo coloca 160 municípios sob risco potencial de tempestades nesta terça. Segundo o órgão, mudanças rápidas nas condições do tempo podem provocar chuvas intensas, rajadas de vento, alagamentos de ruas, transbordamento de mananciais, queda de árvores e danos à infraestrutura urbana e rural.

Entre as cidades incluídas estão Goiânia, Aparecida de Goiânia, Anápolis, Trindade, Senador Canedo , Rio Verde, Jataí, Itumbiara , Catalão, Caldas Novas , Pirenópolis , Formosa , Cristalina , Luziânia , Novo Gama e Valparaíso de Goiás .

A previsão indica possibilidade de chuva em todas as regiões do estado. Os maiores volumes previstos para terça são de até 30 milímetros na região leste, 25 mm nas regiões norte, oeste e central e 20 mm no sudoeste e no sul.

Em Goiânia, o Cimehgo prevê 8 mm de chuva, com temperaturas entre 19°C e 32°C. Em Jataí e Rio Verde, as mínimas podem chegar a 16°C, enquanto Anápolis deve variar entre 19°C e 29°C. Cristalina tem previsão de 15 mm de chuva e temperaturas entre 17°C e 29°C.

Goiânia registrou volumes diferentes de chuva entre as regiões da cidade nesta segunda-feira (7), segundo o Cimehgo — Foto: Diomício Gomes/O Popular

De acordo com André Amorim, a possibilidade de chuva permanece mais significativa até quarta-feira (9). A partir de quinta-feira (10), as precipitações ainda podem ocorrer, mas devem ficar mais esporádicas e irregulares.

O meteorologista explicou que a frente fria está se afastando em direção ao oceano, mas a nebulosidade associada a outros sistemas, somada às temperaturas ainda elevadas, mantém condições para a ocorrência de tempestades isoladas.

A irregularidade já aparece nos registros deste domingo. Dados enviados pelo Cimehgo mostram que, entre 0h01 e 16h26, Cristalina registrou 44 mm, o maior volume entre os pontos monitorados apresentados. Pilar de Goiás teve 30,2 mm, Novo Gama chegou a 25,2 mm e Bonfinópolis registrou 22,4 mm. Em Goiânia, uma estação na Região Norte marcou 16,4 mm, enquanto outros pontos da capital tiveram volumes bem menores, o que reforça a distribuição desigual das chuvas.

Passagem de frente fria provoca leve queda nas temperaturas em Goiás, mas não há previsão de frio intenso, segundo o Cimehgo — Foto: Diomício Gomes/O Popular

Apesar da passagem da frente fria, não há previsão de frio intenso em Goiás. Segundo André, o principal efeito do sistema é aumentar a instabilidade e provocar uma redução moderada nas temperaturas máximas e, em menor intensidade, nas mínimas.

Nesta segunda-feira (7), Jataí e Rio Verde começaram o dia com cerca de 16°C, após a entrada de ar polar na sequência da frente fria. Segundo o Cimehgo, o ar frio não tem força suficiente para avançar sobre Goiás e provocar uma queda acentuada das temperaturas.

As máximas devem permanecer um pouco mais baixas entre terça e quarta-feira por causa da nebulosidade e das chuvas. Depois, com a perda de intensidade do sistema, a tendência é de elevação gradual das temperaturas e retorno aos padrões anteriores.

articles.title: No ápice, ato com Flávio Bolsonaro reúne 28,5 mil pessoas na Paulista, aponta metodologia da USP | G1
articles.standfirst: Estimativa feita pela Monitor do Debate Político e pela More in Common aponta público de até 32 mil pessoas no pico, às 16h32. Manifestação ocorreu nesta segunda-feira (7).
articles.summary: Estimativa feita pela Monitor do Debate Político e pela More in Common aponta público de até 32 mil pessoas no pico, às 16h32. Manifestação ocorreu nesta segunda-feira (7).
articles.body:
O ato de campanha do presidenciável Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e seus apoiadores nesta segunda-feira (7) na Avenida Paulista, em São Paulo , reuniu 28,5 mil pessoas no seu ápice, segundo apontou a metodologia do Monitor do Debate Político da USP/Cebrap e da More in Common.

Com margem de erro de 12%, a estimativa indica que o público ficou entre 25,1 mil e 32 mil pessoas às 16h32, horário de pico. A contagem é feita a partir de fotos aéreas, analisadas por um software de inteligência artificial.

Conforme o monitor, foram tiradas fotos em três horários (15h15, 15h44 e 16h32). Para a contagem de público, 12 fotos tiradas às 16h32 foram selecionadas.

"As imagens cobriram toda a extensão do ato, sem sobreposição. A mesma metodologia vem sendo usada desde agosto de 2022 para calcular o público de diversos eventos políticos", afirmou o Monitor.

Em 2024, 45,4 mil pessoas estiveram na Paulista. Já em 2022, foram 32,7 mil pessoas em São Paulo e 64,6 mil pessoas no Rio de Janeiro. Não houve protesto oficial em 2023.

Flávio Bolsonaro, a esposa, Fernanda, e o pastor Silas Malafaia em ato na Avenida Paulista — Foto: THIAGO MIYASHIRO/PERA PHOTO PRESS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Por volta das 13h30, grupos com bandeiras do Brasil e vestidos de camisetas amarelas começaram a se concentrar na Avenida Paulista. Apoiadores também chegaram com faixas contra o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), principalmente contra o ministro Alexandre de Moraes.

O ato teve como mote as frases "Fora Lula, Fora Moraes". Durante seu discurso, Flávio ressaltou que o ato de 8 de janeiro foi uma farsa, criticou o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal, e ressaltou propostas para a segurança pública e saúde pública.

🔍O Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) já condenou 29 réus acusados de participar da organização criminosa que tramou o golpe de Estado em 8 de janeiro de 2022, em quatro ações penais. Sete deles já cumprem as penas – entre eles, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

Flávio começou seu discurso relembrando que seu pai, Jair, foi esfaqueado em 6 de setembro de 2018 há oito anos. "7 de setembro seguinte eu estava com ele, lutando pela sua vida na Santa Casa de Juiz de Fora enquanto cada um de vocês estava já nas ruas lutando pelo Brasil. Ontem, completaram 8 anos e ele está mais vivo do que nunca."

Para Flávio, Jair Bolsonaro recebeu uma segunda facada, que são os atos golpistas de 8 de janeiro . "Deram uma segunda facada em Bolsonaro. Essa farsa que foi 8 de janeiro. Essa farsa que condenaram um homem correto, um homem honesto, um homem que tem Deus no coração, por crimes que ele não cometeu. Foi a segunda facada", afirmou.

" Por providência divina, a missão que Bolsonaro passou para o filho primogênito, eu estou encarando mesmo que a minha vida esteja em risco e fazendo campanha com colete à prova de bala porque sei do que a esquerda é capaz. Eu faço campanha com colete à prova de bala porque sei que o povo brasileiro é o colete do Brasil, que defende nossa democracia. Vão tentar uma terceira facada, não só em mim, mas nos meus aliados, eu estou avisando."

Em relação à crise no Supremo Tribunal Federal, o candidato fez críticas ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes.

"Nós temos que proteger o STF de Alexandre de Moraes, aquela laranja podre. O Supremo não é Alexandre de Moraes. A magistratura não é Alexandre de Moraes".

Em seguida, falou sobre suas propostas para segurança pública e saúde. "A partir de janeiro do ano que vem, vou declarar guerra aos narcoterroristas. PCC e Comando Vermelho vão ser declarados terroristas. Eles estarão presos ou neutralizados pela polícia. Eu vou trabalhar para reduzir a maioridade penal, cortar impostos, ter castração química de abusador de mulher, e ladrão de celular vai ficar preso no mínimo 8 anos."

"A saúde pública vai ser padrão Einstein. O nosso SUS vai ser padrão Einstein com nosso ministro. Vai ser um Brasil que não depende de político para levar comida para dentro de casa. A minha candidatura é de protesto, para configurar que o Brasil tem jeito, tem futuro. Eu vou cuidar do Brasil", ressaltou.

Apoiadores de Flávio Bolsonaro na Avenida Paulista nesta segunda-feira (7) — Foto: Gustavo Honório/g1

O governador de São Paulo e candidato à reeleição, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), também participou da manifestação. Mais cedo, ele não foi ao desfile cívico-militar de 7 de Setembro realizado no Sambódromo do Anhembi, onde foi representado pelo vice, Felicio Ramuth (MDB).

Na Paulista, ele pediu voto para Flávio e senadores da direita e disse que "absolutamente ninguém está acima da Constituição. Senador nenhum está acima da Constituição. Magistrado nenhum está acima da Constituição. Ministro nenhum está acima da Constituição. Governador nenhum está acima da Constituição. O presidente da República não está acima da Constituição. Ninguém está acima da lei".

O prefeito de São Paulo, Ricardo Nunes (MDB), foi um dos primeiros que discursou pedindo votos para Flávio, Tarcísio, além de Guilherme Derrite (PP) e André do Prado (PL) para o Senado.

Derrite também participou do ato, ao lado de André do Prado, Sergio Moro (PL), candidato ao governo do Paraná, e de Valdemar Costa Neto, presidente do PL.

"Quero declarar a independência do Brasil a partir de 2027 contra o crime organizado no Brasil. Ou os criminosos mudam de país, ou serão presos ou neutralizados no Brasil. Ninguém aguenta mais", disse Derrite.

"Só tem um jeito. O Jair Bolsonaro vai ficar preso mais 10 anos se o Flávio não for eleito. Se o Flávio for eleito, Bolsonaro estará com a gente no dia seguinte. Estamos juntos para a vitória", ressaltou Valdemar.

Nikolas Ferreira também discursou e afirmou: “Fora, Moraes. Escute, Alexandre de Moraes, vamos tirar seu sorriso debochado. Ano que vem não vai ser Lula que vai indicar quatro ministros do STF, vai ser Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio é o único candidato capaz de tirar o PT.”

A Polícia Militar usou bombas de gás lacrimogêneo para dispersar um grupo de manifestantes da esquerda na Avenida Paulista. Segundo a SSP, na região da Rua Peixoto Gomide com a Alameda Santos, um grupo tentou invadir o espaço destinado a aos apoiadores de Flávio, e PM e GCM intervieram para conter as partes.

De acordo com o boletim de ocorrência, houve necessidade de intervenção policial para evitar um confronto entre os manifestantes. Para dispersar o grupo e restabelecer a ordem, a PM fez uso de agentes químicos e de força, conforme o procedimento operacional padrão.

A SSP informou que não foram registrados incidentes graves e que o policiamento permanece na avenida para garantir a segurança e o direito à livre manifestação.

articles.title: Douglas Ruas propõe qualificação profissional no ensino médio do RJ | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato ao Governo do Rio de Janeiro pelo PL foi ao desfile de 7 de setembro, nesta segunda-feira, no Centro do Rio, onde conversou com eleitores.
articles.summary: O candidato Douglas Ruas defendeu a integração na segurança e a expansão de escolas cívico-militares no Rio de Janeiro durante o desfile de 7 de setembro.
articles.body:
O candidato ao Governo do Rio de Janeiro pelo PL , Douglas Ruas , foi ao desfile de 7 de setembro, nesta segunda-feira, no Centro do Rio, onde conversou com eleitores.

Durante a agenda, ele defendeu a proposta de montar um gabinete permanente do governo do estado junto com a união, para integrar as ações na área de segurança pública. Ruas falou também de reforçar a atuação das forças armadas na fiscalização das divisas e da costa do Rio de Janeiro para restringir a entrada de armas e drogas.

Douglas Ruas também falou do projeto de expandir o modelo de escola cívico-militar no estado. A intenção é passar de 17 unidades para 200. O diferencial dessas escolas, segundo o candidato, é o ambiente escolar organizado, com disciplina e respeito ao professor.

O candidato também disse que, se for eleito, pretende promover a qualificação profissional a partir do primeiro ano do ensino médio para conectar a educação ao mercado de trabalho.

Candidato ao Governo do Rio de Janeiro pelo PL foi ao desfile de 7 de setembro, nesta segunda-feira, no Centro do Rio — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

"Eu quero que os nossos jovens saiam da escola com diploma e com uma profissão. Vamos fazer isso respeitando as vocações regionais, em parceria com o setor privado, para que os nossos jovens possam se qualificar naqueles postos em que existam as oportunidades no mercado de trabalho", comentou Ruas.

articles.title: 'Unwise' for legal professionals to give character references, says NI's top judge
articles.summary: Dame Siobhan Keegan was speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme in a wide-ranging interview.
articles.body:
It is "unwise" for members of the legal profession to give character references, the Lady Chief Justice has said.

Dame Siobhan Keegan said she intends to have her sentencing group look at character references amid concerns from victims that they have no opportunity to challenge them in court.

Earlier this year, the Law Society chief executive, David Lavery, provided a character reference for a cousin convicted of serious sexual offences .

On Tuesday members of the Law Society are expected to vote on whether they have confidence in Lavery.

In a wide-ranging interview with BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme, Dame Siobhan said she thinks there is a "discussion" to be had on character references.

"The law does not stipulate that a judge must take into account character references," she said.

"But I know that character references do appear in cases. I think there's a number of elements to this.

"It's unwise for certain people to give character references to start with and I think that has come to pass in a number of circumstances."

Reflecting on the use of character references, Dame Siobhan said the "transparency" of the process could be an issue for victims.

She added that "maybe we have to think about a better way of dealing with this issue".

Political issues 'nothing new' for courts

When asked about how tough sentencing in Northern Ireland is Dame Siobhan said there can be a "knee jerk reaction".

It comes after politicians have called for tougher sentences after sentencing has been handed down in the courts.

Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows asked the director of public prosecutions (DPP) to review the sentence given to a carer who took and shared "demeaning" videos of patients .

He also wrote to the DPP after a man was spared an immediate custodial sentence after causing grievous bodily harm to his three-week-old daughter.

Dame Siobhan said: "I think there is actually an obligation on our politicians and our media and people to just step back and take a breath and think about the importance of maintaining public confidence in the system by accurately and reflectively commenting on sentencing."

Dame Siobhan also told Good Morning Ulster that "any court will be uncomfortable" with getting dragged into politics.

Last month, a decision by the Parades Commission to impose restrictions on a proposed Orange Order parade at Drumcree in Portadown was quashed in the High Court .

The High Court also heard earlier this year that there were no plans by the Department for Communities to implement an Irish language strategy before the next assembly election.

Dame Siobhan said the political arena is a "difficult area for judges to navigate".

"We're not involved in policy making. We interpret the law.

"But at the end of the day, the courts are here for people to have adjudication on issues that are important to them."

Although it is nothing "new", she said political issues "really should be worked out in another arena".

"Politicians should work this out. People should work this out but we'll do our job if we have to and we will answer the legal question, that's what we do, we answer the legal question."

When discussing violence against women and girls, Dame Siobhan said she is concerned about the number of cases that are before the courts.

"I think it's really positive that there is an executive policy on this and I think it's a good sign. But it continues.

"I've always said it's a social issue, it's a cultural issue, I think it's a man's issue because the perpetrators are by and large men.

"I honestly think that more needs to be done in terms of education about boundaries and relationships in local communities and I actually think local community leaders have the opportunity to help on this," she added.

"We've got to weed out misogyny at every level and we've got to look at how we as a society stand up to this type of behaviour which is still part and parcel of the work I see every day.

She said she thinks misogyny in society "must fuel some of this type of offending".

articles.title: 'I performed on stage to get my first job' - the firms turning recruitment into competitions
articles.summary: Applicants have to pitch their ideas on stage in front of a panel of judges and an audience. But is this exciting or unfair?
articles.body:
Yumi Liberman was up on stage in front of a panel of judges and an audience of 300 people, and she had to perform.

But rather than singing, dancing or playing a musical instrument, she and two friends were in an auditorium in London in 2024 to pitch their business idea, hoping to secure a full-time job with cosmetics giant L'Oreal.

"It reminded me of when I used to do competitive sports growing up and the pressure would get heavy," says Liberman, now 24. "But somehow you just get into flow mode."

She and her friends had got through to the UK final of Brandstorm, an international competition run by the French company, where young adults outline their product and business ideas.

Their proposal for a haircare app saw them crowned UK winners and they went on to that year's global final in Paris where they came third.

While only members of the team that finished first automatically got full-time jobs, Liberman had so impressed senior figures at the company that she managed to secure a place on its marketing management traineeship, with a full-time position at the end.

Turning recruitment into X Factor-style competitions, with jobs as the prize, generates publicity and buzz for companies. But for the young people involved, is it exciting - or unfair?

In the current global economic environment, youth unemployment is higher than the national average in many countries, as companies are reluctant to take on new staff. In the UK the unemployment rate for young adults is 16.2%, compared to the overall level of 4.9%.

Competitions like L'Oreal's can offer hope. But the vast majority of the 380,000 people around the world who applied for it this year, up 58% from 240,000 in 2025, didn't win anything.

L'Oreal told the BBC that its Brandstorm competition works well because it helps the company attract a wider range of potential new recruits, including young people who wouldn't necessarily have thought of applying for a job at the firm.

Yet while Liberman says she enjoyed the formal competition structure, others who have been through similar recruitment competitions are critical.

Melissa Alcruz now works in marketing for a US real estate business based in New York City, but in the past she did the same job for TV channel MTV.

While at MTV she competed in an internal competition for a promotion that she says was referred to as a "bake-off". Candidates had to come up with sponsorship and marketing campaigns, and then pitch to a room of seven people.

"This is intimidating, even for a seasoned professional. I ultimately got the job, but even though I won I disliked the process," says Alcruz.

She points out that she already had a demanding full-time role at the company, and was then "expected to complete several substantial projects" for the competition in her spare time.

MTV's current parent company, Paramount Skydance Corporation, has been asked for a comment.

Former recruitment consultant Katrina Collier, now an author, speaker and recruiter trainer, is concerned that competition-based recruitment processes that potentially require candidates to give up lots of their time for free can create "economic discrimination".

"Not everyone can take time, possibly months, to participate in the challenges for the chance to secure one of a limited number of roles," she says. "Does that mean only people from financially strong backgrounds proceed?

"Is that leaving talented applicants who don't have the bank of mum or dad, for example, unable to take part?"

Jamie Kohn, senior director for talent acquisition at research firm Gartner, reasons that competition-based hiring formats are here to stay because employers find it easier to evaluate candidates than via the traditional interview method.

But she agrees that organisations need to be cautious about how much they ask of the jobseekers. "And they should focus on providing feedback… so candidates build their capabilities even if they are not selected."

For psychologist Amanda Potter, her concern is that recruiting via competition events tend to favour extroverts, and therefore put quieter personality types at a disadvantage.

"Does this approach encourage all types of people to apply, or would certain types of people avoid these assessment methods?" she says. "This could result in an organisation [ending up] full of ambitious, competitive people who want to win, possibly to the detriment of others."

However, Liberman, who lives with severe dyslexia, argues that going through a typical recruitment process and related assessments would have been more challenging for her.

It has also meant that she managed to avoid any time spent unemployed after finishing university. Instead, she has gone straight into her chosen field, something she can't say about all of her peers.

"I have a lot of friends coming from extremely reputable backgrounds, extremely educated people who have applied to over 1,000 jobs, and have been jobless."

articles.title: Trump threatens to stop sale of Canadian Bombardier jets in US
articles.summary: The threat against one of Canada's largest companies comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has warned Canadian aircraft company Bombardier that it can no longer sell in the US unless it moves its manufacturing there.

"NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. "If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank'."

The move comes amid an escalating trade war between the two neighbours, and hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs are set to be imposed on $20bn (£14.7bn) worth of US goods.

In a statement, Bombardier underscored that it employed thousands of American workers and said it valued its partnerships with American companies.

The BBC has reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney's office for comment.

It is unclear how Trump intends to block Bombardier from doing business in the US.

The Montreal-based company already operates a factory in the US state of Kansas that builds special mission military planes, and employs 3,500 American workers.

It also operates sites in Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, DC and New Jersey.

About half of its fleet – 5,100 aircraft – is operated by Bombardier customers based in the US.

In a statement on Monday, Bombardier did not address Trump's threat directly, but said its operations "create tens of thousands of US jobs through the company's growing American footprint".

"Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees," its statement said. "Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country."

Bombardier's jets are built at facilities in Canada, the US and Mexico, according to the company's website. They also comply with the North American free trade agreement signed by Trump during his first term, known as CUSMA in Canada and the USMCA in the US.

The company is one of Canada's largest, having contributed C$7.4bn ($5.4bn; £4bn) to the country's GDP in 2024, according to a report commissioned by Bombardier.

It is also one of the largest employers in Quebec's manufacturing sector.

In a post on X on Monday, Quebec premier Christine Fréchette called the company "a source of pride" for her province and "a flagship of our economy".

She added that she has reached out to Bombardier CEO Éric Martel and offered her government's full support.

On Trump's threat, Fréchette wrote: "I will not respond to provocation with provocation."

"Quebec will not allow anyone to dictate where our companies must produce in order to access a market."

Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed late last month after Canada walked away from the negotiating table, after which the US imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of presenting last-minute terms that were "unfair" and "uneconomic", while US officials accused him of refusing to sign a deal for political reasons because of Trump's unpopularity in Canada - an accusation he denied.

articles.title: Tukaram Mundhe: Maharashtra food safety officer who is a social media star
articles.summary: Tukaram Mundhe has gone viral after a series of aggressive inspections of restaurants to detect hygiene lapses.
articles.body:
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.

One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.

They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.

At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.

Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.

His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.

"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.

The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.

Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.

But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.

An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.

"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.

Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.

In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.

"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.

But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.

The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.

Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.

And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.

By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.

Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.

"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".

Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.

The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.

However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.

Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".

Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.

"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.

Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.

His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.

In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.

The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".

The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?

Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.

For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.

"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.

He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.

"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."

The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.

Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.

Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.

But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.

"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.

The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.

For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.

Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.

"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

articles.title: Eiffel Tower shut by staff strike over female workers being moved for religious visit
articles.summary: The mayor of Paris said an investigation would be launched into the incident, which left female employees "humiliated", according to a union representative.
articles.body:
The Eiffel Tower was closed on Monday after staff went on strike over female workers being removed for the visit of a Hindu religious group, workers and management said.

A delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the landmark in the French capital on Saturday.

Staff union representative Diane Davoine says as they arrived at the monument, women were told to move.

"During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there," she told Reuters. Davoine also said management had since apologised to workers over the incident.

"So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated," Davoine said.

She added: "Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again."

Société d'Exploitation de la tour Eiffel (SETE), the company that operates the monument in Paris, confirmed the delegation had asked the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women", according to the AFP news agency.

The firm told AFP that "these conditions should not have been accepted".

They added they "were not in line with SETE's values, nor with the principles of equality between men and women".

SETE president Ariel Weil said: "It is clearly not an acceptable practice.

"I restate the Eiffel Tower's commitment to republican values and to the equality of men and women."

The BBC has contacted the Union Confédération générale du travail (CGT) for a response.

BAPS consecrated its first major temple in France on Sunday, in the suburbs of Paris.

In a statement on X, the BAPS temple in Paris said their trip was "arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others".

It apologised "for any pain or inconvenience caused", adding "we believe in the universal values of mutual respect and service".

On its website, BAPS describes itself as a "spiritual, volunteer-driven fellowship dedicated to improving society" through Hindu values.

It has temples in major cities around the world, including London, Los Angeles and Sydney.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said there would be an investigation into the circumstances of the visit.

"I am taking note of the anger expressed by the employees of the Eiffel Tower, and I want to tell them that their discontent is legitimate," he wrote on X.

"Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city. It must be applied everywhere, for everyone."

French hard-right leader Marine Le Pen said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited'."

Former centre-right French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal, who has said he will run for the presidency next year, said: "In France, no culture, no belief, no worship, nothing nor anyone can come to dictate to women their place."

Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."

articles.title: Iran war live: Qatar warns of ‘industrial catastrophe’ if crisis continues
articles.summary: An average of 10 ships transited Strait of Hormuz daily over past 10 days, the lowest level since May, Kpler data shows.
articles.body:
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Mohammed Al-Ansari, has told US media that opening the Strait of Hormuz is a priority, as the world faces an “industrial catastrophe” if the crisis continues.

An average of 10 commodity ships transited the strait per day over the past 10 days, marking the lowest level since May following US and Iranian strikes on tankers, Kpler data shows.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Port in a storm' and 'Megxit means Megxit'
articles.summary: Immigration protests, Harry and Meghan, and UK-Israel relations dominate the front pages on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Several of Tuesday's papers reflect on the anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth. Metro's headline is "port in a storm", explaining that police were injured and vehicles damaged as hundreds of protesters blocked efforts to bring ashore 120 migrants.

The Sun says the " anger of decent, law-abiding folk " is rising. "Now they try to stop the lifeboats " is the Daily Mirror's take on events, adding that the "mob" targeted "RNLI heroes".

The Daily Express urges the government " not to ignore public anger over illegal migrants", although its editorial stresses the paper agrees with the police that "violence has no part to play in protest".

The Times looks ahead to the government's expected announcement of a trade ban affecting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The paper says retaliation by Israel is likely, as is sharp criticism from the US. The Guardian reports that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will also say that the government will take a "more active" approach in supporting the Palestinian cause .

The i Paper reports the Treasury is to introduce a new ISA to help people buy their first home, and that it will not have an age limit. It is believed that the details are likely to be set out by Chancellor John Healey in his upcoming Budget.

Many of the papers lead on the King clarifying that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex remain private citizens, after their recent move back to the UK. " No return to the Firm " is the Daily Telegraph's headline. The Daily Mail says the King has put "Harry and Meghan in their place ". "Megxit means Megxit" declares the Sun .

And the Daily Mirror is one of several papers to have picked up on criticism of US President Donald Trump's proposed new uniform for his Space Force . The paper says the look, which features a fitted tunic, peaked cap and knee high boots, have drawn comparisons to a "sinister Star Wars-villain style outfit". The menswear writer Derek Guy is quoted as saying it is the kind of costume designers make to point out "who are the bad guys in a space movie". The Daily Star's headline is " storm bloopers ".

articles.title: Police forces failing investigation basics, report says
articles.summary: His Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary said too many victims are not receiving the quality of service they should expect.
articles.body:
Many police forces in England and Wales still need to make improvements in the way they investigate crime and other "basics" of policing, according to His Majesty's Chief Inspector of Constabulary (HMIC).

In her annual report, Michelle Skeer also said too many victims were not receiving the quality of service they should expect.

Forces continue to struggle when it comes to gathering evidence, identifying and progressing lines of inquiry, and keeping victims updated on their cases, she added.

There was progress in neighbourhood policing and in some of the work carried out by regional organised crime units that focus on offenders across multiple local police force boundaries, the report said.

The report continued that the greatest strength of policing is its workforce, with the vast majority of officers showing professionalism and courage.

HMIC inspects all 43 police forces in England and Wales on a two-year cycle.

Out of 13 forces assessed in the current cycle, including Merseyside, Cumbria, and Devon & Cornwall, none received a good or outstanding rating for investigating crime or providing a safe and lawful custody environment.

The other forces assessed were Suffolk, Staffordshire, Thames Valley, West Yorkshire, Northamptonshire, Surrey, Wiltshire, North Yorkshire, Humberside and Kent.

The report says "too many forces still weren't getting the basics right or providing the public with a consistently good service in the areas that matter most to victims".

Beyond weaknesses in investigations, the report highlights gaps in how forces respond to the public, including delays in handling emergency and non-emergency calls, and in response times to incidents.

It also raises concerns about the safeguarding of victims, noting inconsistencies in recognising vulnerability and failure to properly deploy resources appropriately when people are reported missing.

Skeer said it was a "pivotal moment for policing" and "there are still areas where performance is not good enough".

"If managed correctly, I firmly believe that reform presents a significant opportunity to deliver a better service for both the public and those working within policing," she added.

The HMIC report said that evolving crime and threats mean officers deal with more complex and resource-intensive cases.

But the government's planned reforms, including the creation of a National Police Service to take over counter-terror and fraud investigations could alleviate some of the pressure facing local units, Skeer wrote.

Policing minister Sarah Jones said: "Our plans will tackle the long-term challenges in the policing system and bring it into the modern day.

"We are investing in more neighbourhood policing, raising standards and making better use of technology to make sure local policing works for local people."

Responding to the report, the charity Victim Support said: "Police forces are undoubtedly under immense pressure, but they must get the basics right."

Chief executive Katie Kempen added: "It is unacceptable that victims and survivors are paying the price for police failings. Every victim of crime deserves to be treated with respect, to be given access to justice, and to have their needs identified and met."

Growing financial pressure is repeatedly pointed to as increasing the strain on police forces.

Cleveland's police's Chief Constable, Victoria Fuller, recently told the BBC her force has been understaffed and under resourced for years.

"We have got the highest crime rate in the country. We've had the largest decrease in officers in the country since 2010.

"As a police force, if you were to look at the multiple indices of deprivation, our police force is number one. So we absolutely need more, we need more resources."

An extra £2m targeted funding has since been designated to help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime.

Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026-2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash.

The annual HMIC report comes just months after a different publication by the Police Leadership commission found the system for identifying and developing leaders was too weak, with chief constable roles in England and Wales often attracting a single suitable candidate.

The landmark independent review warned police leadership is not consistently of a high enough standard and requires a fundamental overhaul.

It also pointed to low morale and motivation within the service, recommending reformed recruitment and promotion processes.

articles.title: Iran increases gasoline price for its heaviest consumers as economy struggles
articles.summary: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran early Tuesday introduced a higher price for its heaviest users of gasoline, state media reported, in the latest economic pinch caused by months of war.
articles.body: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran early Tuesday introduced a higher price for its heaviest users of gasoline, state media reported, in the latest economic pinch caused by months of war. It’s the second such hike since December. Such gas price increases can be sensitive and contribute to inflation. An increase in 2019 sparked nationwide protests and a crackdown that reportedly killed over 300 people. Without specifically mentioning the war with the United States, the government’s announcement cited the “current situation,” adding that the extra money from the price increase will be given to households. Under the new system, people buying more than their quota of 110 liters (29 gallons) of gasoline a month now must pay 100,000 rials (about 7 cents) per liter, or twice as much as they have been paying since December. Iran still has some of the world’s lowest gasoline prices, but the price increase adds to daily pressures for many of the country’s more than 90 million people. Already, the currency has been dropping to record lows, and purchasing power has weakened. On Monday, the U.S. dollar was trading at 2.22 million rials. Keramat Veis Karami, the CEO of the state oil distribution company, on Monday said the new gasoline rate would affect 15% of consumers, the official IRNA news agency reported. The CEO said consumption reached a record high at 145 million liters (38 million gallons) per day in August, while domestic production capacity was 122 million liters per day. The rest of the supply is imported. Raising prices can help calm high consumption, which experts have blamed on aging cars and spare parts in Iran as well as insufficient public transportation. But experts also say increases in gasoline prices will lead to higher inflation in a country that’s already struggling with an annual inflation rate of about 67%, according to the country’s statistics center, a government agency. Cheap gasoline has been viewed for generations as a birthright in Iran, sparking mass demonstrations as far back as 1964, when a price increase forced the shah to put military vehicles on the streets to replace those of striking taxi drivers. Iranians react to the gas price hike An hour after the new pricing went into practice, two of eight gas stations visited by The Associated Press were closed to regulate the price rate of the pumps. The six others were active, and a dozen cars were in line in each. Security was tight around the filling stations and both uniformed and plainclothes police were visible around. In the queue, Asghar Rahimi, a 34-year-old Tehran resident, said the price increases will not stop. “The tiny amount cannot help government to manage problems like poverty and unemployment,” Rahimi said. “This was the first step. In coming months, they need to raise it again.” Another resident, Ali Salari, 55, feared the raise in price will affect prices of other goods, including bread and meat. “It has been that way ever since government manipulated gas prices,” Salari said. Tehran citizen Hamid Mirzei, 43, said food prices have kept rising and a grocery trip just for staples, like beans and lentils, can cost up to 100 million rials ($73). “Life has become difficult for all of us. Even basic groceries are becoming unaffordable,” Mirzei said. “If gasoline prices go up as well, things will only get much worse,” he added.

articles.title: American family missing in apparent crash of small plane off Bahamas coast
articles.summary: Two grandparents and two grandchildren were onboard, according to the family.
articles.body:
A search is underway for an American family of two grandparents and two grandchildren who are missing after their small plane apparently crashed off the Bahamas coast Monday, according to the U.S. Coast Guard and Bahamian officials.

"At approximately 2 p.m. the Royal Bahamian Defense Force requested Coast Guard assistance following a report of a downed airplane with 4 people aboard approximately 15 miles off Andros Island, Bahamas," the Coast Guard said in a statement Monday evening, adding that they were assisting Bahamian authorities with the search.

"Police on the island of Andros are coordinating efforts to locate an aircraft believed to have crash-landed off the coast of Red Bays, North Andros," the Bahamas Police said in a statement, identifying the plane as a "PA-34 Piper five-seater aircraft, bearing tail number N212ML" which "departed Great Harbour Cay at approximately 11:12 a.m." with four people on board.

"Air Traffic Control subsequently lost contact with the aircraft approximately 13 miles west of Andros Island," the Bahamas Police statement said, adding that poor weather had postponed the search for the family for an unspecified time.

A family statement provided to ABC News identified the passengers as Mario Lamar Sr., 80; Lili Lamar, 79; Sofi Sosa, 28, and Christian Sosa, 22. Mario Lamar is "an experienced pilot with more than 40 years of flying experience," according to the family statement.

The aircraft was "bound for Miami Executive Airport, formerly Tamiami Airport, and its last known contact was at approximately 11:04 a.m. near the western side of Andros Island," the family statement said.

The family asked for Bahamian officials, the U.S. Coast Guard and "all appropriate local authorities to work together and deploy every available resource to locate the aircraft and its four occupants as quickly as possible."

"The Lamar and Sosa families are deeply grateful to everyone participating in the search and to those who have reached out with support," the statement said.

ABC News' Rachel DeLima contributed to this report.

articles.title: Prince George to start school at Eton College
articles.summary: The 13-year-old will follow in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, by attending the elite private school.
articles.body:
Prince George is taking another step in growing up with his first day at Eton College.

He is following in the footsteps of his father, the Prince of Wales, who also attended the historic school in Berkshire.

The 13-year-old prince will become a boarder at the elite private school, which has taught 20 British prime ministers and where fees are around £65,000 a year.

As the oldest child of Prince William and Catherine, George is second in line of succession to the throne.

There had been speculation about which school Prince George would attend when he finished at independent prep school Lambrook in Berkshire, with a number of private schools being suggested.

But a traditional option was chosen, with Prince George following his father, uncle Prince Harry, and great uncle Earl Spencer in attending Eton College.

Prince George will now become a boarder, with the school having 25 boarding houses, with each having approximately 55 pupils, looked after by residential staff headed by a house master.

The school is also not far from the prince's family home in Windsor.

"Some boys take to boarding like a fish to water; others take a minute to settle in," writes the Good Schools Guide about Eton College, which says the school provides each boy with a private single room.

Melanie Sanderson, the school guide's managing editor, said Eton has "spectacular facilities and spacious grounds".

"Yet despite its ancient buildings, it is a modern school with a progressive outlook.

"Most 13-year-old boys arriving there in September cannot possibly know what adult life holds for them.

"Prince George, however, faces a very particular future and his parents, with an unrivalled choice of schools available to them, have decided that an Eton education represents the best preparation for life as a modern working royal," she said.

Among recent politicians to have attended Eton have been Lord David Cameron, Boris Johnson, Kwasi Kwarteng and Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg.

Old Etonian celebrities include Eddie Redmayne, Dominic West, Damian Lewis and Tom Hiddleston.

Prince William, interviewed when he was aged 18, had spoken of enjoying his time at Eton.

"I've really enjoyed being able to go about Eton as just another student," he said in June 2000.

articles.title: UK weather: Drought and hosepipe bans remain despite wettest week since early February
articles.summary: Parts of England and Wales have seen more rain than any other week since early February but are still in drought.
articles.body:
In the last few days of August and start of September, more rain fell than any other week since early February, according to the Environment Agency.

Despite the change to more unsettled and wetter conditions, all of Wales and most of England remains in drought.

And water companies are reminding customers that temporary hosepipe bans are still in force despite the rainfall and decreased demand with the cooler weather.

More rain is in the forecast this week and while that will be welcome, sustained rainfall is needed to reverse drought conditions.

While we had a brief return of summer heat over the weekend for some, the weather since the start of September - and meteorological autumn - has been more unsettled.

According to figures from the Environment Agency (EA), in the week from 28 August to 3 September, rainfall totals ranged from 26mm in south-east England to 48mm in central England.

However, the National Drought Group said that water storage "continued to decline at most reservoirs".

There has been no change to the EA drought status or the temporary use bans in force across ten water company areas.

While there has been less demand for water due to the cooler and wetter weather, "further significant rainfall is needed" to return to normal conditions the EA suggests.

Summer 2026 was UK's hottest on record, Met Office says

Why on average it rains more in August than September

In the first week of September there has been a big variation in rainfall across the UK.

For parts of Scotland we've already seen half the average September rainfall in the first 7 days of the month.

Prestwick, South Ayrshire for example has had 47mm compared to the whole month average of 79mm - or 59% of the average.

However, southern England and south Wales have been largely dry with locations in East Sussex, Buckinghamshire and the Isle of Wight recording less than a millimeter of rain - or 1% of the average September rain.

Those rainfall totals will increase slightly on Tuesday as rain spreads south-east across much of England and Wales.

Parts of the Midlands and eastern England could get a few millimetres with up to around 15mm expected around southern counties of England.

Showers will continue to move in across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England along with some strong winds.

Gales are expected in western Scotland but blustery conditions will be felt widely around northern and then even eastern areas of England into Wednesday.

Temperatures this week will be around the early September average of 17 to 21C.

It may start to warm up slightly later this week with temperatures in the south-east up to the mid-20s Celsius.

The long-range forecast doesn't currently show any sign of significant rainfall across England and Wales needed to alleviate drought conditions for the next month at least.

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv one day after visit by Witkoff and Kushner
articles.summary: Russia  pounded Ukraine’s capital Kyiv with ballistic missiles on Tuesday morning, one day after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the region in an attempt to kickstart stalled peace talks.
articles.body: Russia pounded Ukraine’s capital Kyiv with ballistic missiles on Tuesday morning, one day after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the region in an attempt to kickstart stalled peace talks. Explosions rang out in the city early Tuesday local time, according to a CNN reporter in Kyiv, in a signal the agreed three day-halt on attacks as Washington’s emissaries visited on both country’s capitals was over. Ukrainian officials said the combined attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. Six people were wounded as a result of the attack, which also damaged residential buildings, according to Kyiv officials. Kyiv’s mayor Vitali Klitschko had earlier said people had been trapped inside a residential building, and that the attacks had sparked fires across the city, including at an educational institution. Due to the scale of the Russian attack, military aircraft were put in the air by neighboring Poland to protect its airspace, the Reuters news agency reported, citing the country’s armed forces. On Sunday, Witkoff and Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, met with Ukrainian officials in Kyiv, one day after holding intensive meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as Washington renews its push to end the years-long war. “Substantive progress was made, including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks,” Witkoff said on X following the talks, though no major breakthroughs were announced. Russia and Ukraine had agreed to pause attacks on each other’s capitals for the duration of the weekend of diplomacy, which came after months without significant progress toward resolution. The 72-hour truce expired on Tuesday. The reprieve came after weeks of intense Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital, including a daytime strike on the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service on Friday –– the first time the building had been hit during the conflict. That strike was seen as a major escalation, and a sign that Kyiv is increasingly unable to defend its key assets against Russian attacks as it struggles with critical shortages of interceptor missiles. Ukraine has also ramped up its aerial attacks in recent months, striking targets deeper into Russian territory. On Tuesday morning, the governor of the Russian city of Saratov said a Ukrainian drone attack hit civilian infrastructure in the city and wounded some people in a message on Telegram, Reuters reported. articles.title: Ukraine's chief prosecutor resigns over call centre corruption scandal
articles.summary: In his resignation letter, Ruslan Kravchenko denied the allegations against him, saying he did not want his office "to be used as a tool in political confrontation".
articles.body:
Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko has resigned over corruption allegations related to illegal call centres in the country.

It follows a search of his offices over the weekend by Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators, who said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office.

In his resignation letter, Kravchenko said he did not want his position to be used as a "tool for political confrontation", and referenced an earlier post in which he rejected the claims as "unsubstantiated".

Corruption scandals have plagued Kyiv throughout the war against Russia, with accusations levelled at several members of President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.

According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".

The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.

Kravchenko released a statement on Sunday evening dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated", and denied any wrongdoing.

He tendered his resignation a day later, thanking Zelensky and the Ukrainian parliament for their "trust". The Ukrainian president is yet to comment publicly on the resignation.

Despite the creation of two Ukrainian anti-corruption bodies, Nabu and Sap, over a decade ago, corruption continues to be a significant problem in the country.

In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap.

Kyiv's European partners expressed alarm at the announcement, with ambassadors from the G7 group of nations warning it could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union.

Ukraine is an EU candidate country, a status it was granted on condition it mounted a credible fight against corruption.

Zelensky reinstated the freedom of the two anti-corruption bodies as a result of the backlash, but questions have persisted over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.

Last month, Nabu said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering .

A senior official in Zelensky's office alleged to be involved was sacked.

In an interview with the BBC last month, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the president needed to be asked about his awareness of potential corruption among his closest team.

"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions," he said.

During his time in office, the 35-year-old was credited with heading a drive against corruption.

Since his dismissal in mid-July, after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces, he has been outspoken against what he has called a "systemic crisis of governance" in Ukraine.

However, he has emphasised that he has no evidence that Zelensky is personally involved in corruption.

"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity," Federov told the BBC.

articles.title: Panama Canal may cut ship traffic further as El Niño strengthens
articles.summary: Canal authorities may further reduce ship traffic if a strengthening El Niño worsens the country’s drought.
articles.body:
Panama could impose further cuts on the number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal, an official said, as a strengthening El Niño raises fears of water shortages at one of the world’s busiest maritime trade routes.

The warning from the new administrator of the Panama Canal Authority, Ilya Espino de Marotta, on Monday came after the government declared a nationwide state of emergency over El Niño on August 26.

The canal, which handles 5 percent of global maritime trade, has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 34 starting on September 4.

A further reduction will start on September 15, when the limit will be 32 ships.

Espino, who took over as administrator of the Panama Canal Authority on Monday, told the AFP news agency that restrictions could be tightened again if the drought does not subside.

She said she was not ruling out the possibility that in February or March, the limits “could be reduced to 29 or something similar”.

She said rainfall over the coming months would determine whether further restrictions are needed.

“Depending on how much rain falls in September, October and November – the three critical months – that will determine whether I need to lower any slots further in January, February or March,” she told the Reuters news agency last week.

The restrictions are not expected to become as severe as during the 2023-24 drought, when daily crossings fell as low as 22.

The Panama Canal depends on freshwater to operate the locks that raise and lower vessels travelling between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. Water comes mainly from the artificial Gatun and Alajuela lakes, which are replenished by rainfall.

An average transit consumes about 200 million litres (about 53 million gallons) of water.

That dependence makes the 80km (50-mile) canal particularly vulnerable to prolonged dry weather, and levels in both reservoirs have already dropped with the onset of El Niño.

This year’s El Niño – which affects weather patterns and pushes up global temperatures – is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.

Apart from reducing the number of vessels transiting the Panama Canal, authorities have also reduced their maximum draft, from 15.2 metres to 14.6 metres (50 feet to 48 feet).

Draft ⁠is the depth of water a ship needs to float safely. A lower draft limit means vessels may have to carry less cargo to pass through the canal.

The disruption comes at a sensitive time for global shipping.

The Panama Canal’s importance has increased as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East has fallen sharply amid the US-Israel war on Iran. Some vessels have recently paid more than $1m at auction to secure transit ‌slots through the canal.

Panama is betting on a new reservoir at Rio Indio – a river in the country’s centre – as a longer-term solution.

The project is intended to provide water for canal operations and more than half of Panama’s population for the next 50 years, but it is expected to take five to six years to complete.

Espino, the new administrator, told Reuters that the reservoir would “ensure that the canal never again has to resort to lowering the draft or reducing the number of transits”.

articles.title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1,300 people
articles.summary: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.
articles.body: KATHMANDU, Nepal — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals. Monday was the 13th day since the flooding, which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency. In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed. Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release. The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff. Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done. In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris. Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood. Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris. “We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.” Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.” Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding. Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects. Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

articles.title: Climber dies in fatal fall on Colorado 14er south of Aspen
articles.summary: A 21-member rescue team was dispatched to the remote mountain after nearby hikers witnessed the climber fall and officials determined the injuries were not survivable.
articles.body: Officials in Colorado said a climber suffered a fatal fall Sunday after scaling a towering peak south of Aspen. The tragic incident occurred on Castle Peak, which reaches a steep elevation of 14,272 feet in the Elk Mountains, according to Mountain Rescue Aspen. Responders said rescue team members reached the climber by 4 p.m. after the Gunnison County Sheriff's Office was notified of a fallen climber. However, officials "determined the individual had sustained injuries that were not survivable." NORTH CAROLINA CLIMBER AIRLIFTED AFTER PLUNGING 20 FEET DOWN GORGE, SUSTAINING SERIOUS INJURIES The fall was apparently witnessed by nearby hikers, including Rebecca Rees, who recounted the incident in a statement posted to Facebook. "Unfortunately, we witnessed the event. It has been an extremely sad and terrible afternoon for all involved. He did not survive," she said. Rees said a bystander, identified as Robert, even scrambled toward the climber immediately after the fall, putting himself at risk in case there was still a chance of survival. She added that the victim ultimately "wasn’t alone" in his final moments. NOVICE CLIMBER SURVIVES 1,500-FOOT DROP ON CALIFORNIA'S MOUNT SHASTA AFTER HELICOPTER RESCUE DELAYED BY CLOUDS Rees said the rescue crew responded at a commendable speed. Despite the remote location, helicopter and ground teams reportedly reached nearly 13,000 feet in under two hours on a holiday weekend. According to Mountain Rescue Aspen, officials used off-highway vehicles and helicopters to reach the remote area. After a helicopter located the fallen climber, it returned to Aspen to pick up additional rescue personnel before taking them to the high-elevation area near the peak. MOUNTAIN CLIMBER SURVIVES TERRIFYING 500-FOOT FALL IN CALIFORNIA'S SIERRA NEVADA, NIGHT STRANDED ON LEDGE A total of 21 rescue members were sent into the field, and officials safely recovered and evacuated the deceased climber from the mountain shortly after 8 p.m. Rees said the responders showed extraordinary compassion throughout the recovery effort. articles.title: Popular TV host, media star faces hanging after conviction in major synthetic drug trafficking case
articles.summary: Sarah Khalifa was among 12 defendants sentenced to death after prosecutors accused the group of manufacturing and trafficking synthetic narcotics.
articles.body: A popular Egyptian TV host on Saturday was sentenced to death by hanging in a major drug case that accused dozens of suspects of forming an organized criminal group to manufacture and traffic synthetic drugs. Sarah Khalifa is among 12 defendants facing execution for their alleged roles in the operation, including importing materials used to produce narcotics, according to state-backed media Ahram Online. Capital punishment in Egypt is carried out by hanging for civilian convictions. Khalifa is a media personality, beauty clinic owner and former TV host who has appeared on several Egyptian television channels. Local outlet Masrawy reported that she previously hosted the Egyptian crime show "Mission Impossible." Khalifa, who currently has more than 2.5 million followers on Instagram, was reportedly arrested in Cairo in April 2025 as part of the investigation. DOCTOR AND SON ACCUSED OF RUNNING DANGEROUS SIDE-BUSINESS SCHEME IN NEW YORK The case involved a total of 28 defendants who were charged with forming an organized criminal group, as well as possessing unlicensed firearms and ammunition, Ahram Online said. Twelve were sentenced to death, nine received life sentences and seven were acquitted of all charges. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION CRACKS DOWN ON BRAZIL'S BIGGEST DRUG GANGS WITH ‘GLOBAL TERROR’ DESIGNATION The group allegedly operated like a production and distribution network, with members assigned different roles. Some were responsible for importing raw materials, while others manufactured and distributed the synthetic drugs, the prosecution said, according to reports. The group was also accused of storing materials and manufacturing drugs in a residential property. More than 750 kilograms, or roughly 1,653 pounds, of synthetic narcotics and raw materials were seized during the investigation, prosecutors said, according to reports. The case against Khalifa and the other defendants relied on statements from 20 witnesses, along with technical and digital evidence, including messages, photographs and videos that prosecutors said documented the alleged criminal activity, according to Ahram Online. articles.title: IAEA warns over Iran nuclear access as Western powers push UN referral
articles.summary: UN nuclear watchdog urges Iran to cooperate, as Western powers push to refer its nuclear file to the Security Council.
articles.body:
France, Germany, the UK and the US are pressing the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to report Iran to the UN Security Council, as the nuclear watchdog warns that it remains unable to verify Tehran’s nuclear material more than a year after losing access to key facilities.

IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told the agency’s Board of Governors on Monday that Tehran had provided no information during the latest reporting period on the status of its declared nuclear material or facilities, and inspectors had been unable to conduct on-site verification.

“It is more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge” over previously declared stocks of uranium enriched to as much as 60 percent at facilities hit in US and Israeli attacks in June 2025, Grossi said.

He described the lack of information and access as a proliferation concern that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency”, calling on Iran to restore effective cooperation with the IAEA.

The nuclear watchdog’s warning comes as the four Western powers seek support for a draft resolution at the 35-member board that would send the Iran issue back to the UN Security Council (UNSC) for the first time in two decades, according to Reuters.

The proposed text asks Grossi to transmit the resolution, previous board decisions and his latest report to the UNSC and General Assembly. It also calls on Iran to provide the information and access required by inspectors.

Iran has rejected the move and maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Western governments were again turning to the IAEA after failing to achieve their objectives elsewhere.

“Whenever they run out of options, they turn to the agency and Grossi,” Baghaei said at his weekly news conference on Monday.

He argued that restrictions facing inspectors were a consequence of US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities and that it was unreasonable for those governments to blame Tehran for the resulting loss of access.

Baghaei warned that Iran would take “necessary measures” if the Western powers pursued the resolution.

The draft has not yet been formally submitted to the board, and negotiations over its wording are continuing. Even if it is approved, any concrete action at the Security Council could face opposition from Russia and China, two of the five permanent veto powers.
